response.text: Most of these instructions are assuming that you really do just want to take care of the imps child. But the truth is some people like the power of frightening something and a few would like the job to work better after therapy. So it is possible that you ignored some of the above and are thinking “I can just have the child out for a second”. And then you get your kick out of the child being scared and in fear. But all you really did was feed some part of yourself that wanted it to be scared. So if this is you then please leave the child alone for now.

response.text: It’s important to point out that in this post I am assuming that you want to be good to your inner child. It is possible that you might enjoy scaring your inner child, or belittling it, or want to “fix” it so it becomes a better worker bee. If that’s the case, you need to deconstruct your adult self first, before embarking on inner child therapy.

response.text: Don’t practice the same thing again without knowing what you’re trying to get out of it (and how you’d know if you got it). You might end the practice feeling great with all kinds of insight but if you’re not solving the original problem, you’re wasting your time. If you find that what you’re doing isn’t connecting in a useful way, or only seems to be helping you engage in more self-monitoring while making everything else worse in your life, then try something else (while still keeping what’s helpful).

response.text: Do whatever it is that needs to be done (usually this will be safety related). At the start of the next round of processing, ask yourself why you are here again. Why has something changed since you were last here? Has something come up that allows you to deal with this differently now, or has something come up that makes you unsure of your last answer? Grief does often repeat itself, and that doesn't mean that the child is asking for something new.

The problem with this exercise is that if you are deep in a child state, you may not be able to access the adult in you to do the work of rebirthing that wounded child. This is much easier if you can access one of the adult roles. If you can’t access the adult in you, you may find yourself in one of the following situations:

response.text:
NB I’ve developed this map more practically in the rest of the method, which is why I’m comfortable publishing this provisional synthesis (parts of which are directly research based, the whole of which is my own):

i) child on her own – orientation and external safety

ii) child with borrowed adult – experience of at least one good adult function, personified by a real/remembered/imagined/symbolic figure

iii) adult as apprentice – with help, adult tries to do at least one part of looking after the child

iv) adult in her own right – adult repeats as many times as necessary, to build up the capacity to summon it at will: offering the child warmth, protection and direction

v) adult in relation to child – adult in charge but not banishing child, child no longer solely responsible for managing life

The child doesn’t need to stop being a child – you just become bigger than the child-state. A useful saying to yourself might be: ‘I don’t need to stop being this child, but I am also becoming an adult…’

response.text:
Sometimes we may notice when we’ve been hooked, before we know what part of us has been hooked. Sometimes it may be a bit later, perhaps after we’ve noticed the tightening in our jaw or the getting involved of our stomach and the writing of half of the text message we really, really shouldn’t be sending. In which case it may be a good idea to forget about finding out who’s hooked for the moment – Child, Protector, past hurt. Our hand may already be reaching for a glass of wine or turning to our phones or forming an opinion about our relationship. Pema Chodron has a great word for this tightening/urge – shenpa.

So, let’s just notice that we’ve been hooked. If we can take a breath or two (or three) and finish what we were doing (assuming no-one is in danger) all the better. If we don’t manage to take the breaths to settle down, we may at least have time to summon enough Adult to be nice to the Child, or Protector to stop us doing something stupid, or simply say to ourselves ‘not yet’.

response.text: Sometimes you'll notice you're hooked before you know which part of you is doing the hooking. Sometimes you won't notice it until you've already tensed up your jaw, or whatever, and until you've already done some part of reacting—until you've already written half the text, for example. It's okay to forget, for the time being, to try to figure out which part it is. Just be aware, as Pema Chödron has explained , that there's a kind of tightening, a kind of "I need to do something" sensation that comes before you finish making up the story. She calls this shenpa .

response.text: Let it sit for a few minutes. Yes, there is a giant conclusion you could jump to right now. But wait! Come back later and figure out how to explain what actually happened, if indeed something really did happen that you want to address. And keep descriptions of what happened separate from what happened inside you ("my stomach was in knots") and what you figured out about the other person ("you are an evil creature"). You can get to that later.

response.text: And stay there for a bit. Later on, when you’re feeling good, you can get curious with yourself and wonder what it was about what the other person did or said that actually felt like a violation. Maybe they did do something violating. Maybe they triggered something in you. But you don’t have to figure it out now in order to get out of the pit of your stomach and get into a happier place. You can always come back and decide later if this other person is actually evil or not.
